questions.q: What is the key difference between a symptom and a root cause in data quality work?
options: They are two names for the exact same thing
A root cause is always a human mistake, never a system issue
A symptom only applies to SQL checks; a root cause only applies to profiling
A symptom is the bad value a rule detected; a root cause is the upstream reason that value exists at all
questions.explain: Cleaning up flagged rows addresses the symptom; root cause analysis finds and fixes why the bad data keeps appearing.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four root-cause categories named in this lesson?
options: Technology
Marketing budget
Process
People
questions.explain: The four categories are people, process, technology, and source data — marketing budget isn't one of them.

questions.q: What does the 5 Whys technique actually involve?
options: Running a rule five times to confirm it's broken
Repeatedly asking "why" until you reach a fundamental, actionable cause, usually around five times
Writing exactly five SQL queries to find a problem
Interviewing five different stakeholders
questions.explain: 5 Whys is a simple iterative questioning technique, not a fixed number of queries or interviews.

questions.q: In the lesson's SQL example, grouping null-email orders by source_system was used to do what?
options: Automatically fix the null values
Narrow down which intake channel was actually producing the bad data, as a lead for root cause investigation
Calculate the average order value
Delete the affected rows
questions.explain: Grouping failed rows by a likely driver (source, channel, date) is a fast way to turn profiling output into root-cause evidence.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what three things should a finished root cause analysis produce?
options: A specifically stated cause, a fix for that cause, and a decision on the backlog of existing bad rows
Just a list of affected row IDs
A dashboard, a meeting invite, and a budget request
A new data quality rule and nothing else
questions.explain: The cause, a fix (usually owned by another team), and a backlog decision together are what feed into Lesson 28's issue management process.
